# Problem 1
```{r import dataset and libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)
data("ny_noaa")
```

## Description 
This dataset contains New York temperature, precipitation and snow data collected from 1981 - 2010. There are `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables including `r names(ny_noaa)`, which describe a day's minimum and maximum temperature, inches of precipitation, snow and/or snow depth. However, about 44% of observations are missing data for minimum and maximum temperature. 

```{r data cleaning }

#creating seperate variables for date
ny_noaa  = ny_noaa |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
mutate(
    year  = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day   = day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax), 
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)
)

#looking at temperature, precipitation, and snowfall for reasonable units

noaa_mean= 
  ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp, mean, na.rm = TRUE))

noaa_median=   
 ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp, median, na.rm = TRUE))

noaa_min=   
 ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp, min,na.rm = TRUE))
 
noaa_max=  
 ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp, max,na.rm = TRUE))

noaa_mean
noaa_median
noaa_min
noaa_max
#converting variables into reasonable units
ny_noaa = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  mutate( prcp = prcp/10,
          tmin = tmin/10, 
          tmax = tmax/10)

#checking my work 
noaa_mean= 
  ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp,mean, na.rm = TRUE))

noaa_median=   
 ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp, median, na.rm = TRUE))

noaa_min=   
 ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp, min,na.rm = TRUE))
 
noaa_max=  
 ny_noaa|>
   summarize(across(tmin:prcp, max,na.rm = TRUE))

noaa_mean
noaa_median
noaa_min
noaa_max


```


Exploring data, looking at precipitation specifically
```{r}
ny_noaa |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = prcp)) + 
  geom_histogram()
#the vast majority of days have no precipitation, but there are some high precipitation days 


ny_noaa  |> 
  filter(prcp >= 1000) # there are 653 observations with over 100mm

ny_noaa |> 
 arrange(desc(prcp)) |>
head()
# there is a record on 1982-08-20 of 2286 mm precipitation, and 1983-04-08 of 2032.5 mm precipitation.  This seems unreasonable. 


#what is the most common value for snowfall
ny_noaa  |>
  count(snow, name = "n_obs", sort = TRUE)
```

__Observations and Adjustments__
Given the summary values of the variables and geography climate of new york, I infer that the variables are initially reported in the following units. 

prcp: 0.1mm (mean= 29.8, max = 22860)

snow fall: mm (mean = 4.98, max = 10160)

snow depth: mm (mean = 37.3, max = 9195)

temperature min: 0.1 Celcius (median = 33)

temperature max: 0.1 Celcius (median = 150)



I have adjusted them to be more interpretable and standardized. 

prcp: mm 

snow fall: mm (no change)

snow depth: mm (no change)

temperature min: Celcius

temperature max: Celcius



There are some unreasonable values, such as highest value of precipitation of 2286mm, and smallest value of snowfall of -13 mm. The tmin min and tmax max is 60 C, which seems unreasonable, indicating the reporting thermometer was broken, as they were both reported from the same location ID: USR0000NGAN and span of time 08-17-2008 through 09-16-2008. 

The most commonly (non missing) observed values for snowfall are 0mm, 25mm, 13mm, and 51mm, and 76mm)

### Plots


For July, it is relatively more stable and less variability than in January, where the ranges are wider. 
For July, the average hovers around 27 C, while in January, it fluctuates around 0 C. 
There are outliers. For January, there was a cold day with a mean_tmax of approx -14C around 1982. For July, there is an outlier around 1988 of a mean_tmax of 14C.   


```{r}
ny_noaa  |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax)
  )|>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax,color = month)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(.~month)
```


Two-panel plot (histogram) showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset
```{r}
ny_noaa  |>
  ggplot(aes(x =tmax, y=tmin)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .1)

```

(ii) a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.
```{r}

#density plot for each year
ny_noaa  |>
  mutate(year = as.character(year)) |>
  filter( 0 <snow & 100> snow ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow)) + 
     geom_density(aes(fill = year), alpha = .5) +
facet_wrap(~year) 

#box plot for each year
ny_noaa  |>
  mutate(year = as.character(year)) |>
  filter( 0 <snow & 100> snow ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow)) + 
     geom_boxplot()  + 
facet_wrap(~year) 

```

# Problem 2

```{r creating datasets}

#importing
accel_df = read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_accel.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() 

covar_df = read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_covar.csv" , na = c("NA", ".", ""), skip =4)|>
janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na()|>
  filter(age >=21) |>
  mutate( #encoding sex and education as factor variable as they are categories
    sex = as.factor(sex), 
    sex = recode(sex, 
                         `1` = "Male", 
                         `2` = "Female"),
    education = as.factor(education),
    education = recode(education, 
                         `1` = "Less than high school", 
                         `2` = "High school equivalent",
                        `3` = "More than high school")
  )

#merging 

nhanes_df = 
  left_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")


```

### Distribution of Sex Among Education Level of Study Participants

```{r}
#table
nhanes_df |> 
  group_by(education, sex) |> 
janitor::tabyl(education, sex) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education Level", "Male", "Female")
  )

#bar graph
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")+
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)),position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Sex Among Edcuation Level of Study Participants", x = "Education Level", y = "Number of Participants")

nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex))+ 
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~education) 

```


The boxplot comparisions of age distribution by sex and education level show that among "less than high school" and "more than high school" groups, age distribution between males and females are relatively similar. "Less than highschool" ranges and medians are higher than "More than high school." 
This is also true for subject counts, as females and males contribute similarly, in both "Less than high school" (27 Male , 28 Female) and "More than Highschool" (Male= 56, Female = 59). "More than High school" is the education level with the most participants. 

For the "High school equivalent" group, males' median and interquartile range of age is lower than of females'. In this group, the females' 75th percentile of age is the oldest among education levels. Subject count distribution is also nonequivalent by sex, with 35 Males and 23 Females. 

### Total Activity by Age and Education
```{r}
# creating variable for total activity variable for each participant
nhanes_df =
  nhanes_df |> 
  mutate( 
    total_time = rowSums(across(min1:min1440),na.rm = TRUE) 
    )

# plot total time
nhanes_df |>
 ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_time)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = sex),alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(aes(color = sex),se = FALSE) + 
  labs(
    title = "Total Activity by Age and Education",
    y = "total activity",
    color = "Sex")+
  facet_grid(.~education)

```

  
Between males and female, the largest difference is among high school equivalent education level, where females have higher total activity at younger ages, compared to males. High school equivalent education level has a total activity peak around age 40, and then total activity decreases with age. 

Less than high school has the most distinct sharpest downward trend, where total activity time decreases with age and sex is similar. There is spike in total activity at 60. 

Among more than highschool, there is a platued trend around 13000 total activity time until 55, where total activity time decreases with age.Here Female activity is consistently higher than males. 

Around age 60, activity trends change across sex and education level. 
Among less than high school, activity begins a steep decrease. 
Among high school equivalent, activity platues for males and increases and then decreases for females. 
Among more than high school, activity begins to decrease. 

### 24-hour activity
```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=10}

#plot 24-hour activity
nhanes_df_pivot = 
 nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "min",
    values_to = "mims" ) |>
   separate(min, into = c("mins", "mins_time"), sep = 3) |>
  select (-mins)|>
  mutate ( mins_time = as.numeric(mins_time))

nhanes_df_pivot |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mins_time, y =mims)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(sex)), size = 1, alpha = .05) + 
  geom_smooth(aes(color = sex),se = FALSE) + 
 labs(
    title = "24-hour activity time courses",
    x = "Hours",
    y = "MIMS",
    color = "Sex") + 
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 360, 420, 480, 540, 600, 660, 720, 780, 840, 900, 960, 1020, 1080, 1140, 1200, 1260, 1320, 1380, 1440), 
    labels = c("1:00", "2:00", "3:00", "4:00","5:00", "6:00", "7:00", "8:00","9:00","10:00", "11:00", "12:00",
               "13:00", "14:00", "15:00", "16:00","17:00", "18:00", "19:00", "20:00","21:00","22:00", "23:00", "24:00"))+ 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))+
  facet_wrap(~education, ncol = 1)

```

Overall the activity trends are similar between sex and between education level. 
Activity is low between 1am - 5am( sleeping), and it consistent around 12 MIMS until it starts decreasing 9pm. 
Among more than high school , we see more outliers compared to other education levels. There are higher amounts of MIMs among females around 8-9:00am, while higher amounts of MIMs around 8-10pm, before and after a typical work day. Among more than high school, females' MIMs tend to trend higher than males'. 
Among the other educational levels, there is not a distinguishable trend between sex. 


# Problem 3 

Importing Data
```{r importing data}

citijan2020_df = read_csv(file = "./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2020, month = "Jan")

citijuly2020_df = read_csv(file = "./data/July 2020 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2020, month = "Jul")


citijan2024_df = read_csv(file = "./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2024, month = "Jan")

citijuly2024_df = read_csv(file = "./data/July 2024 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2024, month ="Jul")

citi_df = 
  bind_rows(citijan2020_df,citijuly2020_df, citijan2024_df, citijuly2024_df) |>
  janitor::clean_names()
```

__Description__

This dataset describes citi bike rides from Jan & July 2020 and Jan & July 2024. With the 4 datasets combined there is a total of `r nrow(citi_df)` observations, with `r ncol(citi_df)` variables including `r names(citi_df)`. 


```{r}
citi_df |> 
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |> 
    count(member_casual, year, month) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = c(year, month), 
    values_from = n, 
    values_fill = 0
  )|>
   knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Membership Status", "Jan 2020", "Jul 2020", "Jan 2024", "Jul 2024")
  )

```

Between membership status, members consistently had more rides than casual riders. 
Between months, July had more rides than January, in every comparision, when matched for year and membership. 
Between years, 2024 had more rides than 2020, when matched for month and membership. 


The 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; including the number of rides originating from these stations.

```{r}

citijuly2024_df |> 
  count(start_station_name,name = "n_rides", sort = TRUE)|> 
  head(n=5)|>
   knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Start Station Name", "Number of Rides")
  )

```


__Median Ride Duration Across Years, Months and Weekdays__
    
```{r}

week_order = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")

citi_df |>
  mutate(weekdays= factor(weekdays, levels = week_order))|>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |> 
  summarize(median =median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x= weekdays, y = median, color=month, group = month))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+ facet_grid(.~year)+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))+
  labs(
    title = " Median Ride Duration Across Years, Months and Weekdays",
    x = "Days of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration")
```

Comparing months between years, 2020 had longer median ride duration than 2024 and a bigger difference between January and July. Overall, median ride duration increased over the week, peaking on saturday. 


__Impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration__
```{r citi2024}
citi_2024_df = 
citi_df |> 
filter(year == 2024) |> #selecting for 2024 only 
  mutate(month= factor(month)) # for using boxplot

citi_2024_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x =month, y = duration, fill = month)) + 
    geom_boxplot()+
  labs(
    title = "month, membership status, and bike type on ride duration distribution",y = "Ride Duration in Minutes")+facet_grid(member_casual~rideable_type)



```

Between months of January and July, ride duration is relatively similar, when compared among bike type and membership status. The largest IQR of ride durations is among casual riders using classic bikes. For member rides, the 75% of rides are short, less than ~20 minutes, thus, casual riders had longer ride durations overall(75% under ~25 minutes).For members, classic bike and electric bike durations are similar, across January and July too. There is a large spread of ride duration outliers among casual electric bike rides in July.
